sections.title: A Blessing over Good and over Bad
sections.html:
The purpose of the blessings is to give thanks and praise to God, may He be blessed, who watches over His creatures at all times. Through the blessings we are reminded again and again that God does not dwell only in the hidden treasuries on high, but rather everything that exists in the world is given life and sustained by Him. And every event that occurs in the world has a spiritual meaning and a Divine purpose. Therefore, when a person merits something new and joyous, he should recite Sheheḥeyanu. And if, Heaven forbid, a disaster befalls him, he should know that this too is with Divine consent, and he should recite Dayan Ha-emet ("the true Judge").

Through the blessings, faith is revealed and spreads in the world, and consequently the life of the one reciting the blessing is also blessed. For the knowledge that God guides the world, and that everything comes from Him and under His providence, gives value to all of life's events. When a person merits something joyous, his joy is deeper, because it did not come by chance but from the hand of Divine providence. And through this he will merit to use properly the abundance he received. And also when, Heaven forbid, a disaster strikes him, he has more strength to accept it when he knows that it has meaning. For even if at present he does not understand what good will grow out of the bad, out of the knowledge that everything God does in the world is all for the good, he will ultimately be able to rise up out of the disaster and build his life. But one who does not believe has nothing but his trouble, and the sadness pierces and penetrates his heart without remedy and without meaning.

One should know that a special joy beyond the ordinary is not needed in order to recite Sheheḥeyanu; rather, even over a small joy that a person newly experiences when buying an ordinary garment, or when eating a new fruit, one must thank God and recite the blessing. There is fundamental guidance in this outlook. Many people wait for some great event that will elevate their lives all at once, and in the meantime their lives are gray and gloomy. But a person who becomes accustomed to notice the small joys in his life and to thank God for them learns to recognize the value of life, which is composed of small details in which great content is hidden, and through this he will merit a full life, rich in content and meaning.

sections.title: Obligation and Option in the Sheheḥeyanu Blessing
sections.html:
The Sages instituted two main types of the Sheheḥeyanu blessing. The first is over festivals, such as Pesaḥ, Shavu'ot and the other festivals, and likewise over mitzvot that have a fixed time, such as the shofar on Rosh Ha-shana, the lulav on Sukkot, and lighting candles on Ḥanukka. This blessing is a complete obligation, for since the sanctified time or the time of the mitzva has arrived, one is obligated to thank God and recite: "who has given us life, sustained us and brought us to this time." The laws of this blessing are explained in the laws of the festivals, and it is not our concern to deal with them in this chapter.

The second type, with which we will deal in our chapter: thanksgiving for good things that are new for a person, such as buying a house, furniture, clothing and jewelry. And likewise over good news, and over seeing a good friend after thirty days in which one did not see him. This blessing is optional, for even one who has experienced new good things and is happy with them, according to most poskim, is not obligated to recite Sheheḥeyanu over them. And all that the Sages said about reciting Sheheḥeyanu over a new house and new vessels means that it is a mitzva to recite the blessing, but there is no sin on the part of one who does not recite it. And some say that whenever a person is happy with the good things over which the Sages instituted Sheheḥeyanu, he is obligated to recite the blessing. And what they said, that this blessing is optional, means that there is no obligation to buy joyous things in order to recite Sheheḥeyanu over them, but one who buys and is happy is obligated to recite the blessing.

And although according to most poskim the Sheheḥeyanu blessing is optional, it is right to recite it at every opportunity regarding which the Sages said it is a mitzva to say it. For it is proper for a person not to lose the precious opportunity given to him to thank and bless God.1

sections.title: Sheheḥeyanu and Ha-tov Ve-hametiv
sections.html:
The Sages instituted two blessings over new and joyous things. The first: "Blessed are You, Lord our God, King of the universe, who has given us life, sustained us and brought us to this time"; and the second: "Blessed are You, Lord our God, King of the universe, who is good and does good." The difference between them is that when the joy belongs to one person, his blessing is Sheheḥeyanu. But when the joy is shared by two people or more, the joy is greater, and they must recite Ha-tov Ve-hametiv, for this is the meaning of the blessing: "who is good" to me, "and does good" to others. For example, a person who bought furniture for himself, such as a table, a chair, a heater or an oven, should recite Sheheḥeyanu. But a couple who bought the same furniture for themselves, since the joy concerns both of them jointly, should recite Ha-tov Ve-hametiv. It is good that one of the spouses recite the blessing and the other answer "Amen", and if one of them recited the blessing alone, the other should also recite Ha-tov Ve-hametiv for himself.

Over buying a new garment that one is happy with, one recites Sheheḥeyanu. And although the husband is happy that his wife has a new dress, and the wife is happy that her husband has a new garment, since the tangible joy concerns only the one who wears the garment, only he recites Sheheḥeyanu.

However, parents who bought a new garment for their child, or received a new garment for him as a gift, and they are happy with it, should recite Ha-tov Ve-hametiv. For since they are responsible for his clothing, they take pride in his nice appearance, they have tangible joy from this, and they may recite the blessing. They should recite the blessing this way until the children reach the age of mitzvot, for until then they are completely responsible for them and their clothing is in accordance with their guidance. And it seems that from the time the children reach the age of ḥinukh (education in mitzvot) (around age six), it is right to educate them to recite Sheheḥeyanu themselves over their new garment as well.2

One who gained a large monetary profit: if he is married and the money goes into the joint account of him and his wife, since they are partners in the joy, they should recite Ha-tov Ve-hametiv. And if he is single, or married and the money goes into his private bank account, he should recite Sheheḥeyanu. And although presumably his wife too will benefit from his having more money, since in practice the money belongs only to him, and perhaps his wife will not benefit from it, he should recite Sheheḥeyanu (Responsa Halakhot Ketanot vol. 1, 196 and 200).

The same applies to a sole heir: if he is single, or married and the money goes into his private account, he should recite Sheheḥeyanu. And if he is married and the money goes into the joint account of him and his wife, they should recite Ha-tov Ve-hametiv.

And if there are two heirs or more who divide the inheritance between them, even if they are single, they should recite Ha-tov Ve-hametiv, since they benefit together from the same inheritance (SA 223:2; BHL s.v. "ve-im").

There is another fundamental difference between these blessings: the Ha-tov Ve-hametiv blessing was instituted over a tangible benefit, such as a new house and new vessels, or an additional wine drunk together (above 7:7). Whereas the Sheheḥeyanu blessing is a more general thanksgiving, which was instituted also over a new joy that involves no tangible benefit, such as good news from which there is no tangible enjoyment (below, halakha 8), and likewise over festivals and mitzvot that have a fixed time.

In any case where there is doubt between the Sheheḥeyanu blessing and Ha-tov Ve-hametiv, one should recite Sheheḥeyanu. For one who is obligated in Ha-tov Ve-hametiv and recited Sheheḥeyanu has fulfilled his obligation, since he thanked God for the good that came to him. But one who is obligated to recite Sheheḥeyanu and recited Ha-tov Ve-hametiv has not fulfilled his obligation, because in his blessing he gave thanks for good that came to two, whereas in truth the good came to an individual.3

sections.title: Sheheḥeyanu over Clothing and Small Gifts
sections.html:
The Sheheḥeyanu blessing was instituted over new things that gladden a person's soul, for example one who bought clothing, vessels, furniture or jewelry, or received them as a gift. But over routine life, such as the monthly salary a person receives, even though its value is much higher than the value of a new garment, one does not recite Sheheḥeyanu. Likewise over the food that a person buys from time to time, even though its price is high, one does not recite Sheheḥeyanu. One can say that for routine life the Sages instituted the fixed blessings that we recite in the morning blessings, in prayer and in the blessings over enjoyment, whereas the Sheheḥeyanu blessing was instituted for something that has newness and joy.

Even over an ordinary garment, such as a nice shirt, whoever is happy with it recites the blessing. And even one who already has many shirts, if he bought a new one or received it as a gift and he is happy with it, should recite Sheheḥeyanu. And even if he bought or received as a gift a used garment, if it is a garment that people take pride in, and he too is happy with it, he should recite Sheheḥeyanu. The same applies to eating utensils, jewelry and the like (SA 223:3).

However, wealthy or indifferent people, whom buying an ordinary garment does not gladden, cannot recite the blessing over it, for how can they say "who has given us life, sustained us and brought us" when they are not happy? But over an important garment, such as a suit or a luxurious dress that gladdens them a little, they should recite the blessing, and if they are not happy at all, they have lost the blessing (Radbaz; MB 223:13).

But most people are happy at buying ordinary clothing, such as a shirt, pants, a nice tie, a skirt, a tallit katan, a nice hat and pajamas, and over every purchase of such a garment they should thank God with the Sheheḥeyanu blessing. Only over buying simple and cheap clothing that people are not usually happy with, such as socks, underwear, a simple head scarf, or a simple T-shirt, one should not recite Sheheḥeyanu. And even a poor person who is very happy at buying them, according to most poskim, should not recite the blessing, for it is not proper to say a blessing over a trivial thing that is not considered joyous in the eyes of most people. But it is proper that he thank God in his own words, or say the blessing without God's name and kingship.

To summarize, two conditions are needed for the Sheheḥeyanu blessing: first, that the one reciting the blessing be happy with the new garment or vessel; second, that it be a garment or vessel that many people are usually happy with.4

sections.title: Winning Money and Grants
sections.html:
One who receives a monetary gift, or won a lottery, or received a monetary inheritance, recites Sheheḥeyanu, and if the recipients are partners, they should recite Ha-tov Ve-hametiv (Berakhot 59b; SA 223:2). But one should not recite a blessing over a regular salary or over benefits and bonuses that it is customary to give employees as part of their work, because there is nothing new in this.

In order to recite the blessing over winning money, the sum of money he receives must be of significance, for there is a difference between winning money and buying or receiving a garment. With a garment a person has immediate joy, and therefore even if its value is low, since in practice he is happy with it, he must recite the blessing. But winning money only makes it possible to buy things (over which he will be able to recite Sheheḥeyanu), and in order for the joy in the money to be real, the sum won must be of significance for the winner.

And it seems that for people of modest means, such as young people who have not yet begun to work, or adults whose situation is tight, five hundred shekels (in 5774) can be considered a large sum, so that if they are happy with it, they should recite the blessing. But people who have more money will be truly happy only if their winnings are larger, and everything depends on their character and their wealth. However, it is not necessary that the monetary winnings be as high as the monthly salary; rather, even one who earns ten thousand shekels a month, if winnings of two thousand shekels gladden him, should recite the blessing.

As we have learned, one should not recite a blessing over a fixed salary or regular profits that a person usually earns in his business. But if he suddenly earned a large, unexpected profit, over and above the usual, even though it is within the framework of his work and business, he should recite the blessing (Halakhot Ketanot 1:200; Seder Birkot Ha-nehenin 12:10).

A poor person who was given a large sum of tzedaka should not recite the blessing, because he feels shame in receiving it. But if he was given a garment and he is happy with it, he should recite the blessing (Eliya Rabba; MB 223:20).

One who receives a monetary grant or scholarship, for studies or for something fine that he did, feels no shame in this, and if the grant is large enough to gladden him, he should recite the blessing. This is on condition that it is a special grant that not everyone receives, but if it is a grant or scholarship given to many as a matter of routine, it is like a salary, in which there is no new joy.

sections.title: The Time of the Blessing
sections.html:
The time for the Sheheḥeyanu blessing is when the joy is new. For example, one who learned that he had earned an especially large sum should recite the blessing when he hears about it. And if he is not sure of the reliability of the report, he should recite the blessing when the money comes into his possession (see below, halakha 8).

Likewise regarding an inheritance, the time of the blessing is after the money enters the heir's account or the apartment is registered in his name. In the past, close to the death of the one bequeathing, people would recite two blessings: Dayan Ha-emet over his death, and Sheheḥeyanu over the inheritance, since according to the law the inheritance passed into his possession immediately (Berakhot 59b). And although the heir would have preferred that his father remain alive, since it was not possible to ignore the benefit and joy that came to him from the inheritance, together with the Dayan Ha-emet blessing he had to thank God for the inheritance. However, today, funds are deposited in the bank and houses are registered in the land registry, and it takes time until the inheritance passes into the heir's possession, and thus it is possible to separate the time of the blessing of joy from the days of mourning.

Over a new garment one may recite the blessing immediately when buying it, and many are accustomed to postpone the blessing to the time of its first wearing. And if at the time of purchase the garment is not fit for use, because it needs to be altered or something added to it, the blessing should be postponed to the time of its first wearing, for then one is happy with it (SA 223:4; MB 17; Kaf Ha-ḥayim 30).

The same law applies to buying a closet: if at the time of purchase it is not fit for use, the blessing should be postponed to the time when one begins to use it. And if it was fit for use at the time of purchase, one may recite the blessing over it at the time of purchase.

Likewise regarding eating utensils that require immersion (tevila), one should not recite the blessing over them at the time of purchase, since they are not yet fit for use. Rather, one should recite the blessing over them when beginning to use them (see Rabbi Akiva Eger 223:3, and MB 22:1 [?]).

One who forgot to recite the blessing over furniture when he began to use it may recite the blessing as long as he is happy with its newness. One who forgot to recite Sheheḥeyanu over a garment at the time of its first wearing has lost the blessing. But if on subsequent occasions he is still truly happy with the garment, for example it is an especially important garment, he may recite the blessing.5

Because of the great necessity of clothing, the Sages instituted that one who puts on a new garment should thank God and recite: "Blessed are You, Lord our God, King of the universe, who clothes the naked." And afterward he should recite Sheheḥeyanu. And if he puts on the new garment in the morning, the Malbish Arumim blessing among the morning blessings applies to the new garment as well, and it is good to have this explicitly in mind (SA 223:4; MB 18. Some are not accustomed to recite Malbish Arumim over a new garment, and so wrote the Kaf Ha-ḥayim 223:32).6

sections.title: A New House
sections.html:
A couple who bought a house, if they are partners in it, must both recite Ha-tov Ve-hametiv. And if the house belongs to one of them and is registered in his name, only he should recite the blessing over it, but since they will benefit from it together, he should recite Ha-tov Ve-hametiv. An individual who bought a house for himself should recite Sheheḥeyanu. But one who rents a house, or one who received permission to live in a house for a number of years, since the house is not his, does not recite a blessing over it (SA 223:3; BHL s.v. "bana"; Ḥatam Sofer OḤ 53).

One should say the blessing when moving in to live in the house. And if a mezuza must be affixed in it, it is good to say the blessing when affixing it, for then the house becomes ready for living (see Rabbi Akiva Eger 223:3). And one who forgot to recite the blessing then should recite it as long as the joy of the newness of the house continues.

Even one who took a mortgage and various loans in order to buy his house must recite the blessing (Tzitz Eliezer 12:19). However, if for this purpose he went into large debts, and he has no steady work, and he fears that he will not succeed in meeting the payments, he should not recite the blessing (Lev Ḥayim 3:52; Kaf Ha-ḥayim 223:18; Ḥazon Ovadia, Berakhot p. 394).

Even one who already has one house, if he intends to live in the new house as well, must recite the blessing over it. But if he bought a house in order to rent it out, or he is a merchant who buys and sells houses, he does not recite a blessing over buying houses. Likewise, a merchant of vessels and clothing does not recite a blessing when he buys them as merchandise (Mor U-ketzi'a 223).

One should also recite the blessing over enlarging a house, or renovating a room in a way that improves it and makes it more comfortable. But one does not recite a blessing over regular repairs or regular painting done from time to time (see MB 223:12).

Residents of a community who built for themselves a building intended to serve the public, since they are partners in it, when they dedicate it, a representative of the public should recite Ha-tov Ve-hametiv on behalf of everyone. Likewise if it is a school, although it belongs to the regional council or to the Ministry of Education, since it is intended for public use, a representative of the public or of the school should recite Ha-tov Ve-hametiv over it. And if they are hesitant to recite a blessing over a building that is not theirs, the one reciting the blessing should put on a new garment, and in this way recite Sheheḥeyanu without doubt. And if they bring two wines, they should also recite Ha-tov Ve-hametiv.

Some say that it is proper for those immigrating to the Land to recite Sheheḥeyanu upon arriving in the Land for the purpose of aliya, and so was the practice of many rabbis. And it is likewise proper for anyone who is happy with his aliya to recite Sheheḥeyanu for having merited to fulfill the great mitzva about which the Sages said (Sifrei, Re'eh 53) that it is equal to all the mitzvot.7

sections.title: Good and Bad News, and Receiving Titles
sections.html:
One who heard good tidings that are good for him and for others recites Ha-tov Ve-hametiv, and if they are good for him alone, he should recite Sheheḥeyanu. And if he heard bad news, he recites Dayan Ha-emet (Berakhot 54a; SA 222:1-2).

For example, partners who invested in a certain thing and learned that their investment yielded especially large profits, over and above what was expected, should each recite Ha-tov Ve-hametiv. And if they received the news together, one may recite the blessing for both, and his companion answer "Amen." And if he has no partner, he should recite Sheheḥeyanu. And if he heard that he suffered a great loss, and he is sad about it, he should recite Dayan Ha-emet (Halakhot Ketanot 1:200; Seder Birkot Ha-nehenin 12:10).

Likewise, if a person was falsely accused, brought to trial and sentenced to punishment, he should recite Dayan Ha-emet. And if he was supposed to receive a large sum, and they did not give it to him, and he sued them in court and won, he should recite Sheheḥeyanu.

Likewise we learned (above 15:9) that one who owned a field in partnership, if the rains had been withheld and they were distressed, and beneficial rains began to fall, each of them should recite Ha-tov Ve-hametiv. And the sole owner of a field should recite Sheheḥeyanu.

One who heard that his son earned an especially large profit, and he is happy about it, should recite Sheheḥeyanu. And although he has no tangible enjoyment from it, we have already learned (above, halakha 3) that only the Ha-tov Ve-hametiv blessing depends on tangible enjoyment, but the Sheheḥeyanu blessing is recited over good news even when there is no tangible enjoyment from it. And if he heard that his son suffered a very great loss and he is sad about it, he should recite Dayan Ha-emet. And even if these things happened to his friend or his rabbi, to whom his heart is very attached, if he rejoices in his joy he should recite Sheheḥeyanu, and if he is sad he should recite Dayan Ha-emet (Ma'amar Mordekhai 222:1; Shulḥan Ha-tahor 222:1; and see Seder Birkot Ha-nehenin 12:7).

One who hears about the death of a worthy person, and is pained by it, must recite Dayan Ha-emet. And although the widespread custom is to recite the blessing only over the seven relatives for whom one sits shiva, in practice, one who hears about the death of a worthy person and is very pained by it should rightly recite the blessing (see MB 223:8).

One who thought that he was about to earn a large profit and learned that he did not earn it, even though he is very sad, should not recite Dayan Ha-emet, because in practice he did not lose anything that was in his possession (BHL 222:2).

If he received news that they decided to raise his salary beyond the customary raise, or that he received an unexpected promotion in rank, he should recite Sheheḥeyanu. Likewise, one who hoped to be appointed to a certain position, and heard that he was chosen, should recite Sheheḥeyanu. And if he forgot to recite the blessing when he heard about it, he may recite it as long as he is very happy with the good news. And if a party is held for him on the occasion of his entering the position, he may postpone the blessing from the time of hearing the news to the time of the party, when he is happiest.

One who was fired from his work, or whose salary was greatly reduced, and he is very distressed about it, should recite Dayan Ha-emet.

One who received news that he passed the driving test successfully, or received a high score on the psychometric exam or another important exam, if he is very happy about it, should recite Sheheḥeyanu. Likewise, one who was accepted for a job he wanted, and he is happy about it, should recite Sheheḥeyanu.

One who received an award of recognition, such as an honorary doctorate, or was chosen to be a rabbi, or finished his studies and is receiving an advanced degree, or received an officer's rank, whoever is happy about it should recite Sheheḥeyanu. The time of the blessing is when receiving the news or at the ceremony. One who recited the blessing when receiving the news and wishes to recite it also at the ceremony should buy a new garment in honor of the event. Some are hesitant to recite the blessing, because sometimes improper pride is mixed into the joy over the award or the appointment, which clouds the joy, and sometimes the appointment is made through corruption, and then it is forbidden to recite a blessing over it. However, in practice, whenever the appointment or award came honestly, it is right that one who is happy with it recite the blessing (see Mor U-ketzi'a 223; Maḥazik Berakha 223:8; Melumdei Milḥama 33:2).

sections.title: Holy Books, a Torah Scroll and a Synagogue
sections.html:
One who buys or receives a new book and is happy with it, whether holy or mundane, recites Sheheḥeyanu. Although some hold that one should not recite Sheheḥeyanu over holy books, since the mitzvot were not given in order to derive ordinary enjoyment from them but in order to become sanctified through them, the halakha follows the opinion of most poskim, that one who is happy with them should recite Sheheḥeyanu.8

One who merited to hire a scribe to write a Torah scroll for him should recite Sheheḥeyanu when he finishes the writing and brings the Torah scroll into the synagogue (Responsa Mahari Bei Rav 62; Magen Giborim 223:3; Arukh Ha-shulḥan 8). Those who are scrupulous hold a meal and bring two wines in order to drink them together, and recite Ha-tov Ve-hametiv over the second wine, having in mind also the Torah scroll in which the congregation rejoices (see above 7:7-8). Some are concerned that perhaps one should not recite Sheheḥeyanu over the scroll, and in order to avoid the doubt they buy a new garment and recite Sheheḥeyanu over it, having in mind also the scroll (Birkei Yosef YD 270:8).

At the dedication of a synagogue, one of the representatives of the congregation should recite Ha-tov Ve-hametiv on behalf of everyone (Maḥazik Berakha 223:1; Magen Giborim 7; MB 11). Some are hesitant to recite the blessing, and in order to avoid the doubt and to thank God, they should hold a celebration and bring two wines, and recite Ha-tov Ve-hametiv over the second. It is also right that one of the participants put on a new garment and recite Sheheḥeyanu over it, and have in mind in his blessing the synagogue as well.

There were great Torah scholars who, when they authored a book, were accustomed to recite Sheheḥeyanu upon its publication. And although the poskim disagreed about this, one who is happy and wishes to recite the blessing may do so (Mor U-ketzi'a 223; Tzitz Eliezer 14:67).

sections.title: The Sheheḥeyanu Blessing upon Meeting a Friend
sections.html:
The Sages instituted that one who sees a good and dear friend after thirty days in which he did not see him, and new joy arises in his heart, should recite: "who has given us life, sustained us and brought us to this time." But if he saw the friend within thirty days, he should not recite a blessing over seeing him, because there is nothing new in it. We learn a great principle from this halakha: that friendship has great value, and meeting a good friend is a meaningful thing, to the point that the Sages instituted a blessing over it.

However, many are not accustomed to recite Sheheḥeyanu when meeting a friend. This is because the blessing was instituted only over meeting an especially good friend whom one is happy to see, and it is difficult for a person to examine in his heart whether this friend of his is an especially good friend. It is likewise difficult to assess whether the level of joy aroused in his heart is sufficient in order to recite the blessing.

In addition, several of the Aḥaronim raised a concern that if people become accustomed to this blessing, there will be people who will be offended when they see that their friends do not recite Sheheḥeyanu over them. And there will be others who, in order to prevent offense, will recite Sheheḥeyanu even over someone they are not happy to see, and will come to a blessing in vain. And there will be flatterers and deceivers who, when they see a person from whom they wish to receive some benefit, will jump up and recite Sheheḥeyanu, in order to prove to him how great, as it were, their love for him is (Ḥesed La-alafim 225:15).

However, as halakha, one should not abolish a blessing that the Sages instituted because of these concerns. And it is right to strengthen the observance of this blessing, which expresses the sacred value in friendship. Nor should a person fear that perhaps he does not know how to measure whether the friend is truly dear, for we are not speaking here of a rare and special friendship that only exceptional individuals merit. Rather, the intention of the Sages is that every person recite the blessing over his good friends. And every ordinary person who is not overly closed has friends who are dear to him, and if he is happy to meet one of them after not having seen him for thirty days, he should recite the blessing.9
One should know that one is not always so happy at a meeting with a good friend. Sometimes a person is preoccupied with his worries, and therefore his heart does not open to joy. And sometimes he has no time to talk at length, and he has no joy from a hurried meeting. In practice, whenever he is not actually happy at the time of the meeting, he should not recite the blessing.

Included in this blessing, of course, are also family relatives who have not seen each other for thirty days: if they are happy to meet, they should recite the blessing. For example, a grandfather who has not met his grandson for thirty days and is happy to see him is commanded to recite Sheheḥeyanu. Likewise a brother with his sister, and the like.

sections.title: Details of the Halakha
sections.html:
Even one who spoke with his friend on the telephone or in a video call during the thirty days, if he is happy when they meet, should recite the blessing.10

One who met a good friend whom he had not seen for thirty days and recited Sheheḥeyanu, and afterward met another good friend whom he had not seen for thirty days, should recite the blessing again, and so too for the third and the fourth. For as long as they are his good friends and he is happy to see them, he should recite the blessing. However, if he saw several of his friends together, one blessing covers all of them (Da'at Torah 225:1).

It is right to institute the practice that when a gathering of friends or a family gathering is held, they honor one of them who is certainly happy to recite Sheheḥeyanu aloud over seeing all the friends or family members whom he has not met for thirty days, and he should intend to fulfill the obligation of all of them with his blessing, and they too should answer "Amen" and intend to fulfill their obligation through his blessing. In this way all of them will fulfill the mitzva of thanksgiving and blessing over all the good friends whom they see at that gathering.

sections.title: The Blessing over a Friend Not Seen for Twelve Months
sections.html:
One who has not seen his dear friend for twelve months and also has not heard about his welfare, to the point that there is some concern that perhaps he is no longer among the living, when he sees him should recite: "Blessed are You, Lord our God, King of the universe, who revives the dead" (Berakhot 58b; SA 225:1).

Seemingly one should ask: at the time of the meeting the friend did not come back to life, so why should we recite "who revives the dead" over seeing him? But a separation of a year creates a real change in the soul. Over the many days the soul concentrates on other things, and the feelings of friendship are forgotten and disappear into the hidden recesses of the soul. Mourning too ends after a year, because a period of a year dulls and causes the earlier feelings to be forgotten. To the point that it appears, according to dry logic that looks only at what is revealed, that after a separation of a year, after the emotion has turned to other areas and other friends, there is almost no possibility of reviving the feelings of friendship. But the truth is that although it appears outwardly that the feelings of friendship have been forgotten, in the depth of the soul the friendship is alive and exists, and immediately with the first meeting it is awakened to life. There is in this fact an allusion to the resurrection of the dead, and therefore at a meeting with a friend about whom one has heard nothing for a year one recites "who revives the dead," to point to the enormous power of the inner life, which can awaken to life even after a long slumber. And in exactly this way we believe that no true longing will remain orphaned; death cannot cancel love, but rather, in the depth of life, in the hidden recesses of the soul, everything remains in existence forever, until the end of days, when all will rise to life and meet again with all their dear and beloved ones (see Olat Re'iya vol. 1, p. 380).

This blessing is hardly recited today, because thanks to the means of communication, a person hears if something happens to his friends during the year, and therefore when they meet they should recite Sheheḥeyanu (Halakhot Ketanot 1:220; Birkei Yosef 225:3).

sections.title: The Blessing over the Birth of a Son and the Birth of a Daughter
sections.html:
Over the birth of a son one recites Ha-tov Ve-hametiv, because this joy is shared by the father and the mother (Berakhot 59b; SA 223:1). If the father and mother are together, one of them should recite the blessing and the other answer "Amen." And if the father is not with his wife who has given birth, the mother should recite the blessing for herself, and the father should recite it when he hears the good news of the birth of his son (Orḥot Ḥayim 1, Se'uda 34).

Over the birth of a daughter they should recite Sheheḥeyanu when they see her for the first time (Rabbi Shneur Zalman, Seder Birkot Ha-nehenin 12:12; MB 223:2). If they are together, one of them should recite the blessing and the other answer "Amen." And if the father is not with his wife who has given birth, the mother should recite the blessing as soon as she sees her daughter, and when the father merits to see his daughter for the first time, he too should recite Sheheḥeyanu. If they did not recite the blessing at the first sight, as long as they are happy and moved at seeing her, they may still thank God and recite Sheheḥeyanu.11

Parents to whom a sick or disabled child was born should not recite the blessing, since they are not happy. But if they are nevertheless happy, they should recite the blessing.

The grandfather and grandmother too, if they are very happy when they see their grandson or granddaughter for the first time, should recite Sheheḥeyanu. Likewise other family members or very close friends, if they are very happy when they see the baby boy or baby girl, may recite Sheheḥeyanu. And even upon hearing the news, one who is very happy may recite Sheheḥeyanu, even though he does not see the newborn baby. And one who recited the blessing upon hearing the news should not recite it afterward upon seeing the baby (Seder Birkot Ha-nehenin 12:7; BHL 223:1).

sections.title: New Fruits
sections.html:
One who sees a fruit that has newly appeared in its season recites Sheheḥeyanu, in order to thank God who renews His world and has made this fruit grow for us in its season. In the past, when many were engaged in agriculture, people were accustomed to recite Sheheḥeyanu when they saw the new fruits, for then they rejoiced in them. And today too, one who wishes to recite the blessing upon seeing a new fruit may do so. However, the widespread custom is to recite Sheheḥeyanu when eating the new fruit for the first time, because most people are happier about its newness when they eat from it (SA 225:3; Levush).

A person may not shut himself off from the abundance that God created in His world, as the Sages said: "A person will in the future have to give an accounting for everything his eye saw and he did not eat." For in this way he belittles the value of creation with its variety of fruits. And some explained that it is because he thereby loses the Sheheḥeyanu blessing that he could have recited over the new fruits (Tashbetz Katan 320). And it is likewise related about Rabbi Elazar that he would save from his money and buy every kind of fruit at least once a year, in order to taste it, rejoice in it and recite Sheheḥeyanu over it (Yerushalmi, end of tractate Kiddushin; MB 225:19).

If so, before eating a new fruit one must recite two blessings: one, Sheheḥeyanu, and the second, Ha-etz or Ha-adama. Some are accustomed to say the blessing over the fruit first (Radbaz and Ḥida), and some are accustomed to say Sheheḥeyanu first (MB 225:11). The one reciting the blessings may choose how to act.

One should not recite the blessing over the fruit while it is still unripe, but only after it has finished ripening and become tasty (SA 225:7). Be-di'avad, if he recited the blessing over it when it was edible in pressing circumstances, he should not recite the blessing again over these fruits when their ripening is complete (MB 225:12). One who forgot to recite the blessing the first time he ate from the new fruit has lost the time of newness, and should not recite the blessing at his second eating (MB 225:13). But as long as he is engaged in his first eating, he should recite the blessing.12

If there were before him two kinds of new fruits, one blessing covers both, even if he does not intend to eat from the second kind. But if the second kind was not before him, even though it was in his house, the Sheheḥeyanu blessing he recited over the kind before him did not exempt the second (see Mishpatim Yesharim 45; Sha'ar Ha-tziyun 227:16; Me'at Mayim 65).

sections.title: Fruits That Are Renewed and Those That Are Not
sections.html:
Over fruits that are not renewed in a particular season, but rather grow throughout the year, or which can be kept fresh throughout the year, one does not recite Sheheḥeyanu. Even one who has not eaten them for a long time should not recite the blessing over them, for the blessing is not over personal joy but over the renewal of the fruit in its season (SA 225:6). Therefore, even in the past people did not recite the blessing over nuts, onions, garlic, potatoes and beets, because they were kept all year.

There are many fruits over which in the past people recited Sheheḥeyanu, because they could be obtained only in a particular season, whereas today they are found in the markets all year, and consequently one does not recite Sheheḥeyanu over them. There are three reasons for this: 1) Today many fruits, such as apples and bananas, can be kept in refrigeration throughout the year. 2) There are kinds of vegetables, such as tomatoes and cucumbers, that can today be grown all year in greenhouses. 3) Through the import of fruits from abroad, many fruits can be supplied throughout the year. For example, today there are pears in the markets all year, with some of the months being imported from abroad.

This is the rule: any fruit that is found in the markets throughout the year in its fresh form, or close to its fresh form, even though there is a season in which it grows, one does not recite Sheheḥeyanu over it. But if there is a certain time when it is not common in the markets, when its season arrives and it newly appears, one should recite Sheheḥeyanu over it. And although these fruits too can be kept in refrigeration or imported from abroad, and can be obtained in some stores throughout the year, since in practice there are months when they are rare, and when they arrive fresh at the market everyone senses their newness, one recites Sheheḥeyanu over them (see Igrot Moshe OḤ 3:34; Ḥut Shani, Inyanei Berakhot 7. And some disagree; see Piskei Teshuvot 225:17, 2).13

sections.title: Two Varieties of One Species
sections.html:
The poskim disagreed regarding kinds of fruit that have several varieties. Some say that one blessing covers all of them (Knesset Ha-gedola and Birkei Yosef), and some say that since there is a significant difference between them, one recites a separate blessing over each of the varieties (Sefer Ḥasidim, Maharil and SA 225:4).

In practice, there are varieties whose differences are so small that only experts distinguish between them, and it is clear that one should not recite Sheheḥeyanu over each of these varieties. And even when the differences are noticeable, in taste and appearance, as long as the difference is not great, because of the doubt one should not recite the blessing. And when possible, it is good to exempt them with the blessing recited over a fruit over which it is clear that one must recite Sheheḥeyanu.

But when we are dealing with varieties that have a great difference between them in taste and appearance, close to the difference between two kinds of fruit, one who is happy at their newness may recite Sheheḥeyanu, for they are like two kinds and not like two varieties. And if in addition they also grow at different times, one should recite the blessing over each variety.14

sections.title: Fruits from Grafted Trees
sections.html:
Some hold that one should not recite Sheheḥeyanu over a fruit that grew on a tree that was grafted from two species, since a transgression was committed with it (Halakhot Ketanot 1:60). And some hold that just as one recites Ha-etz before eating them, so one recites Sheheḥeyanu over them, for although the act of grafting is forbidden, the fruits that grew from it are permitted to be eaten (She'elat Ya'avetz 1:60).

In practice, people are accustomed to recite Sheheḥeyanu over every fruit that newly appears in its season, without being concerned that perhaps it is a fruit that grew on a tree grafted in a forbidden manner. First, because this is the custom, and where there is a custom we are not concerned about a doubt regarding blessings. Second, even if we know that the fruit grew on a grafted tree, there is still a doubt whether the grafting was done in a forbidden manner, for perhaps it is a grafting of two varieties of the same species, in whose grafting there is no prohibition. And it is possible that the grafting was done by a gentile, and some hold that there is no prohibition for him to perform grafting.

Likewise one should recite the blessing over a pomelit (sweetie), which is a combination of a pomelo and a grapefruit, because the way it is created is by cross-pollination and not by grafting tree branches, and in this manner there is no prohibition (Peninei Halakha: Kashrut 3:5).15
